lessons.title: haben — "to have"
lessons.gloss: to have — the twin of English have, and the workhorse the rest of the book leans on

segments.text: German's workhorse verb, and the twin of a word you have said every day of your life.
haben — "to have."
Same word as English have, worn differently. Chop the -en the way you did with machen and the stem is hab-, which is where every form in this chapter starts.
Two syllables, and the first one carries the weight: HAH-ben.
long-a — the a of haben is long and open, the vowel of English father, not the clipped a of hat.
d-t-final — that long a does not survive into every form. Two of them coming up are short and clipped, and both end in a crisp, fully released t.

segments.instruction: "haben" — long a, soft second syllable
the stem on its own — "hab-"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the stem on its own — "hab-"]

segments.instruction: the twins — "haben, have"

segments.text: "haben, haben — to have."
Say "to have." (Haben.) What is its stem? (Hab-.) Is the a long or short? (Long — as in father.) Which English verb is it? (Have.) Next: the stem through the ending machine you already own.

lessons.title: hab- through the machine
lessons.headword: ich habe, wir haben, ihr habt
lessons.romanization: ich habe, wir haben, ihr habt
lessons.gloss: four of haben's six forms come out of the ending machine you already own, with nothing new to learn

segments.text: You own an ending machine: a stem, and -e, -st, -t, -en. Run hab- through it before reading on, and keep what you get.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: four forms you already knew

segments.text: On hab-, the machine is right four times out of six.

Ich takes -e, so ich habe. Wir takes -en, so wir haben — which is the infinitive over again, the way the wir form goes throughout German. Ihr takes -t, so ihr habt. And sie takes -en like wir, so sie haben.

Nothing there is new. Those four are the rule from your first verbs applied to one more stem — so do not read them off the page. Take each ending, put it on hab-, and hear that you already knew the answer.
The chapter is about the other two.
Build each one before you say it — take the ending first, then put it on hab-.

segments.text: "ich habe, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben."

Build "we have" without being given it. (Wir haben.) Build "you all have." (Ihr habt.) Which other form does wir haben match? (The infinitive.) Did you have to learn any of those four, or work them out? (Work them out — the endings were already yours.) How many of the six does the rule get right? (Four.) Next: the first one it gets wrong.

lessons.title: du hast — "you have"
lessons.gloss: you have — the first form where the b falls out and the rule stops working

segments.text: The machine says du plus -st on the stem hab-. Say what that would give, and then hear what German actually says.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: du hast

segments.text: du hast — "you have," to one person you are on familiar terms with.
The rule predicts hab-st. German says hast. The b is simply gone, and the long a goes with it: the vowel is short and clipped now, and the -st lands crisply on the end.

This is not a spelling convenience. It is one of exactly two places in the whole verb where the machine fails, and it is worth meeting on its own so that it is a form you know rather than a form you derive wrongly.
vowel-a — short and clipped, the a of English hat, not the long a of haben. The form is one syllable: hast, rhyming with English mast.
d-t-final — the -st is fully released; German does not soften it.

segments.instruction: "du hast"
the long against the short — "ich habe, du hast"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the long against the short — "ich habe, du hast"]

segments.source: [YOU SAY: what the rule wanted, then what German says — "hab-st … hast"]

segments.text: "du hast, du hast."

Say "you have," informally. (Du hast.) Which letter went missing? (The b.) What happened to the vowel? (It shortened.) What would the rule have predicted? (Hab-st.) Next: the second place the machine fails, and it fails the same way.

lessons.title: er hat — "he has"
lessons.gloss: he has — the second and last form where the b falls out

segments.text: One more break, and then the verb behaves for good. The machine says -t on hab-.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: er hat

segments.text: er hat — "he has." Also sie hat, "she has," and es hat, "it has."
The rule predicts hab-t. German says hat: the same b gone, the same vowel shortened. One syllable, rhyming with English hut rather than hat — the German a sits further back than the English one.
One form covers er, sie and es, exactly as the third-person -t always does. So the two breaks in this verb are neighbours: du hast, er hat, and every other form is the machine.

segments.text: "du hast, er hat."

Say "he has." (Er hat.) Say "she has." (Sie hat.) Which two forms of this verb break the rule? (Hast and hat.) What do both of them drop? (The b.) Next: why they drop it, and the English verb that does the identical thing.

lessons.title: The b that fell out
lessons.gloss: why hast and hat lost their b — and the English verb that lost it in the same two places

segments.text: Hast and hat both lost a b. That is not two accidents.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one shortcut, in exactly two cells

segments.text: Haben keeps its b everywhere except before a -st or a -t ending, where the b drops and the vowel shortens with it.

Say hab-st and hab-t at speed and you can feel why: a b squeezed between a vowel and a hard t is work, and centuries of speakers declined to do it. The consonant wore away and the two shortest forms are what is left.
Now listen to English, which is the same verb:

utterances: person: infinitive. English: have. German: haben.
person: second person, older. English: thou hast. German: du hast.
person: third person. English: he has. German: er hat.

segments.text: English lost the same consonant, in the same two cells, of the same verb — and kept the archaic hast long enough for us to see it. Two languages, one shortcut, inherited together rather than invented twice.

segments.text: "hast, hat — no b."

In which two forms does the b drop? (Hast and hat.) What else changes with it? (The vowel shortens.) Which English form still shows the same loss? (He has — or archaic thou hast.) Next: something to actually have.

lessons.title: einen — "a," when it is the thing you have
lessons.gloss: a, an — the form the word takes for a masculine thing you have, and the first sighting of a system taught later

segments.text: Ich habe … wants something after it. The commonest thing to put there is "a something," and German asks one small question first.
einen — "a," for a der-word that is the thing you have.
Ein is the number one doing a second job, which is exactly what English a is — a worn-down one. German keeps the resemblance visible: ein, eins.
The -en on the end is the part English threw away. German marks a der-word differently when it is the thing being had rather than the thing doing the having, and einen is that marked form:
Ich habe einen Bruder. — "I have a brother."
Der Bruder is a der-word, and he is what you have, so ein becomes einen. Nothing else in the sentence moves.

Take this one as a word for now, not as a system. The system behind it — German's cases — gets a chapter of its own later; this is the first place the book cannot avoid it, because a sentence with haben in it needs something to have.

segments.instruction: "einen"
"Ich habe einen Bruder."
it with the two broken forms — "du hast einen Bruder; er hat einen Bruder"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it with the two broken forms — "du hast einen Bruder; er hat einen Bruder"]

segments.text: "Ich habe einen Bruder."

Say "I have a brother." (Ich habe einen Bruder.) Which word did ein become? (Einen.) Why? (Because der Bruder is the thing being had.) Which English word is ein underneath? (One.) Next: the trap this verb is famous for.

lessons.title: haben is not habēre
lessons.gloss: the famous false cognate — haben is a cousin of capture, and Latin habēre is a cousin of give

segments.text: German haben, Latin habēre. Same consonants, same meaning, and the best false cognate in the business.
Two verbs that look like one word:

utterances: language: German. verb: haben. meaning: to have.
language: Latin. verb: habēre. meaning: to have.

segments.text: They are not related. It is a coincidence, and one of the most famous in linguistics. Follow each one back and they go in opposite directions.
Haben comes from Germanic habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European kap-, "to seize." That root's Latin child is capere — which is where English gets capture, captive, capable and accept.
Habēre comes from a different root entirely, gʰabʰ-, and its English descendant is … give.
So German haben is a cousin of capture, and Latin habēre — the source of French avoir and Italian avere — is a cousin of give. Seizing and giving, which is about as far apart as two verbs get.

This is worth carrying beyond one verb. Resemblance is not evidence. Two words can match in sound and sense and still have nothing to do with each other, and the only way to tell is to follow both back rather than to compare them where they stand.
Most of this book's cousin pairs are real. This one is the control that proves the others were checked.

Are haben and habēre related? (No — a coincidence.) Which English word is haben's cousin? (Capture, from capere.) And habēre's? (Give.) What did haben's root originally mean? ("To seize.") Next: the whole verb, said through.

lessons.title: Practice — the whole of haben
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — the six forms on one page for the first time, four of them free and two of them earned

segments.text: No new words. Four of the six forms below cost you nothing, and the other two have each had a lesson, so this is the first place it is safe to set them out together.

utterances: singular: ich habe. plural: wir haben.
singular: du hast. plural: ihr habt.
singular: er/sie/es hat. plural: sie/Sie haben.

segments.text: Run it aloud and hear where the b goes missing: habe … hast … hat … haben. Four forms carry it, two do not, and the two that do not are the two shortest.

utterances: Hast du einen Bruder? means Do you have a brother?
Ich habe eine Schwester. means I have a sister.
Wir haben Brot und Wein. means We have bread and wine.
Gut! Dann haben wir alles. means Good! Then we have everything.

segments.text: Two things slip in without lessons of their own, because the translation carries them: eine, which is what ein becomes for a die-word, and alles ("everything"). And notice Hast du …? — a question puts the verb first, which is the one move German makes that English needs do for.
